code.title: override vs new

followUps: Hiding is useful when the base method cannot be changed and you need a different shape in the derived API. Example: a library ships Base.Get() returning object, and your Derived adds new string Get(). Versioning is the other case: a base class later adds a method with the same name as yours, and new keeps your method working and silences warning CS0108. Callers must hold the derived type to see it, so use it sparingly.

A virtual or overridden method is called with callvirt, which reads the object's method table and jumps through a numbered slot. A new method gets its own fresh slot (or, if non-virtual, is called directly with call or callvirt and no slot lookup). The compiler picks by the static type, so a.Speak() on a base-typed variable still uses the base slot, which an override rewrites but new leaves alone.

code.title: Abstract base with template method behind an interface

followUps: They make interfaces closer to abstract classes: an interface can now carry a body for a member, so it can offer shared behaviour and be extended without breaking implementers. Still, no fields or constructors, so state stays in classes. Choose an interface plus default members for a capability that grows over time, and keep the abstract class when subclasses share state or a constructor. Example: adding Warn() to ILogger with a default no longer breaks the 50 existing loggers.

Because multiple base classes would bring the diamond problem: two parents with their own fields and constructors, and it is unclear which copy of the data is used. An interface has no state, so a class can implement many without that ambiguity; if two members clash, you implement one explicitly. Single inheritance also keeps object layout simple: a derived object is the base layout plus extra fields. Example: class Stream2 : Base, IDisposable, IAsyncDisposable is fine; two bases are not.

code.title: Construction order and a virtual call from a base constructor

followUps: They behave the same as ordinary constructor parameters for this order: a primary constructor argument is captured when the chained constructor runs. A base primary constructor call class D(int x) : B(x) runs Base's initialisers and constructor first (after D's field initialisers), then D's remaining initialisers that use captured parameters have been applied. So a virtual call from B's constructor still sees D's fields as default unless they are assigned from a parameter in an initialiser. Do not rely on it.

Java prints the base constructor first, and Java's derived field initialisers run only after super() returns. So a virtual call in Base sees the derived field as default (null or 0) even for a field with an initialiser like String s = "x". C# differs: derived field initialisers run before the base constructor, so the same field would already be "x" in C#, as the program shows with d. Only fields set in the constructor body stay unset in both.

code.title: Equals without GetHashCode breaks HashSet

followUps: It gets lost: the item sits in a bucket chosen by its old hash, but lookups now compute a new hash and look in a different bucket, so Contains returns false and Remove fails. The object stays stuck in the set, counted but unreachable. Example: key hashed with Id = 7, then Id set to 8; set.Contains(key) is false. Hash only immutable fields, or never change a key while it is in a collection.

The default ValueType.Equals may use reflection to compare every field, and it boxes both operands; the default GetHashCode may use only the first field, so structs with an equal first field collide heavily. A Point(1,2) and Point(1,9) can land in one bucket and turn lookups into a slow scan. Fix: implement IEquatable<T>, and override Equals(object) and GetHashCode() with HashCode.Combine(X, Y).

code.title: Explicit interface implementation

followUps:
A subclass cannot call or override the explicit member directly, because it is not visible on the class. The base class author should make it forward to a protected virtual method, then subclasses override that. Example: void IPrinter.Run() { RunCore(); } plus protected virtual void RunCore(). Without this hook, the subclass can only re-implement the interface itself in its own class declaration, which replaces the base mapping.

void IPrinter.Run() { RunCore(); }
protected virtual void RunCore() { }

Use a generic method with a constraint, void M<T>(T x) where T : IComparable<T>. The JIT creates a specialised version for each struct type and calls the interface member directly (constrained call), so the struct is not boxed. Calling through a variable of type IComparable boxes a copy each time. Example: sorting 1 million int values via IComparable allocates 1 million boxes; the generic constrained version allocates none.

code.title: Composition: swappable strategy plus a decorator

followUps: Composition costs more types and more wiring. You write small interfaces, forwarding methods and constructor parameters, and a reader must follow calls across several objects instead of one class. There is more indirection (a virtual call each hop) and more objects to create. Forwarding every method of a wide interface is boilerplate. Example: a Checkout with three collaborators needs three constructor parameters, but each can be swapped or faked in a test. Worth it when behaviour varies; not for a fixed IS-A tree.

A container resolves the constructor dependencies and builds the chain for you, so you do not write new Logged(new Retrying(new Real())) by hand. You register the real service and wrap it, for example with Scrutor's Decorate<IShipping, Logged>() or a factory lambda, and the order of registration sets the order of wrapping. Lifetimes (singleton, scoped) are managed too. The cost is that the chain is no longer visible in one place, so keep decorators few and document the order.

code.title: sealed override and sealed types

followUps: Because the sealed class is not meant as a base, so a record that is open for inheritance is the safer default for a data-modelling type: record inheritance was designed in (records can derive from records, with EqualityContract keeping equality correct). Sealing would break modelling like record Person with record Student : Person. Records do not seal themselves, but you can add sealed, and then you gain the same speed-ups. Record structs are implicitly sealed because structs cannot be inherited.

It is a .NET 8 optimisation: the runtime records which concrete type is most common at a virtual or interface call site while code is running. When it recompiles the hot method, it inserts a type check, "if the object is exactly type X, call X's method directly (and inline it), else do the normal virtual call". Example: a loop where 95% of items are Circle then calls Circle.Area inline with one comparison. It gets some of the benefit of sealed without sealing.

code.title: Virtual slots, base.Method and callvirt null check

followUps: Because base.Method() must run exactly the base class's own code, not whatever the object's real type overrides, so the compiler uses call (a direct, non-virtual call) instead of callvirt. With callvirt it would look up the object's slot and reach the override again, giving an endless recursion. Example: in B.F(), base.F() goes straight to A.F. The null check of callvirt is not needed since this is never null there.

It adds a new slot at the end of the derived type's table, and the base slot keeps pointing at the base implementation. So there are two slots with the same name: calls through a base-typed variable use the old slot and get the base code, while derived-typed code uses the new slot. Example: class B : A { public new virtual void F() } and class C : B { public override void F() }: an A reference to a C still calls A.F, a B reference calls C.F.

code.title: Default interface method stand-in with an extension method

followUps: You cannot call a default implementation from an overriding class in C#, because there is no base(IFoo).M() syntax (it was cut from the language). Workarounds: put the default logic in a static helper or a protected method that both the interface default and the class call. Example: static string Format(string m) inside a helper class, the default calls it, and your class calls the same helper before adding more. The default is simply replaced, not extended.

Static abstract members (C# 11) let an interface require static members, such as static abstract T Zero or operators, so generic code can write T.Zero and a + b. They have no body in the interface and every implementer must provide them. Default instance methods give a body to instance members for old implementers. Example: INumber<T> uses static abstracts for generic maths; IEnumerable<T> default members help versioning.

code.title: LSP violation: Square as Rectangle

followUps: Yes, it is a known compromise: string[] can be used as object[], so code written for object[] may store an int and the runtime throws ArrayTypeMismatchException at that write. A reader expects writes to succeed, so it breaks substitutability, and the check also costs time on every array store. Example: object[] a = new string[1]; a[0] = 5; throws. Generic collections such as IReadOnlyList<out T> are safe covariant types because they cannot write.

They split reading from writing, so a method that only needs to read takes IReadOnlyList<T> and no read-only implementation has to pretend it supports Add. A type promises only what it can do, which is the fix for the Liskov problem. They are also covariant: an IReadOnlyList<string> can be used as IReadOnlyList<object> safely. Example: Print(IReadOnlyList<object> items) accepts a List<string> without any risk of a runtime type error.

code.title: Double dispatch with the Visitor mechanism

followUps: Choose Visitor when the set of types is stable, you add new operations often, and you want the compiler to force every visitor to handle every type: adding a method to IVisitor breaks all implementers at compile time. Choose a switch when the types are few, the logic is small and lives in one place. A switch over an open hierarchy gives no such guarantee, but needs far less code. Example: exporting 8 shape types to JSON, XML and SVG suits a Visitor; a one-off 2x2 collision table suits a switch.

With dynamic, the compiler does not pick the overload; the runtime binder (DLR) looks at the actual types of the arguments when the call executes, and picks the best overload then. That gives double dispatch in one line: Hit((dynamic)a, (dynamic)b). It costs more: the first call at a call site is slow (reflection, then caches the rule), later calls are faster but still slower than a direct call, and mistakes surface only at run time as RuntimeBinderException.

code.title: Value equality by hand, as a record generates it

followUps: Because the generated equality compares the fields, and for a List<T> field that means comparing the reference, not the items. Two records with two different lists holding the same 3 numbers are not equal; the same list object shared by both records is equal. Mutating the list also changes the hash of the record, which hurts when used as a key. Use ImmutableArray<T> and compare with SequenceEqual in a custom Equals, or accept reference equality for that field.

Yes, but only ToString is allowed to be sealed in a record. Add public sealed override string ToString() => ... (C# 10). Without it, a derived record gets its own generated ToString that prints its own extra members, so sealing it keeps the output fixed to the base's format. Example: record Person(string Name) { public sealed override string ToString() => Name; }, and record Student : Person then prints just the name.

code.title: Payment plug-ins: registry plus decorator

followUps: Test each decorator alone with a fake inner object, then test the wiring once. A fake IPaymentProvider records its calls and returns a scripted result; assert that a retry decorator calls the fake 3 times after 2 failures and passes the result on. Then build the real chain with fakes at the end and check the order of effects, for example log first, then retry. Example: fake that fails twice then succeeds, expect 3 calls and a success. A small integration test guards the registration order.

Add a small capability interface next to the main one, such as IPartialRefund with Result RefundPart(decimal amount). A provider that supports it implements both interfaces. Callers check with if (p is IPartialRefund r) r.RefundPart(5m), or the registry exposes a query like Supports<IPartialRefund>(). Others do not change and the core interface stays small. Decorators must forward the capability too, so they should either implement it or you unwrap them first.

code.title: Fragile base class: AddAll double counting

followUps: First pin behaviour with tests, then work in small steps that each keep the tests green. Step 1: find what each level really adds. Step 2: turn the base's overridable behaviour into an interface and pass collaborators in by the constructor. Step 3: move one level's logic into a separate class the child calls, then delete that level. Example: a 5-level tree becomes 2 levels plus 3 strategy objects over a few sprints. Seal the classes you finish, and keep old public types until callers have moved.

They work because the base is designed for it: small, stable, documented, with a clear contract. Stream offers few abstract members (Read, Write, Seek) and builds the rest (CopyTo, async methods) on top, so FileStream and MemoryStream stay consistent. Exception is a data carrier with almost no behaviour to break. Both are a true IS-A, are only 2 to 3 levels deep, and Microsoft controls the base and tests it. Your own deep trees rarely have those properties.
